title: MODULE 06 — API Validation, Error Handling and Reliability

blocks.text: Building an API that works under normal conditions is not enough. A professional backend must also behave predictably when users submit incorrect information, database operations fail, external services become unavailable, or multiple requests arrive simultaneously.
Imagine PrepSpaces has thousands of students accessing its learning platform.
A student submits an enrolment request without a course ID.
A user submits an email address in an invalid format.
A student accidentally clicks the Enrol button five times.
An external AI service stops responding.
An API receives thousands of requests within a few seconds.
A database operation succeeds, but another operation in the same workflow fails.
An API response changes and breaks an older frontend version.
These are not unusual situations. They are normal challenges in backend engineering.

A reliable API must know how to validate requests, communicate errors consistently, prevent duplicate operations, control traffic, handle failures and maintain compatibility as the application evolves.
In this module, you will learn how to develop APIs that remain predictable and maintainable under both normal and unexpected conditions.
The module primarily uses Java, Spring Boot, Spring Validation, Spring Security, PostgreSQL, Redis and Resilience4j.
By the end of this module, you should be able to:
Perform input validation and safe data handling.
Validate request DTOs using Jakarta Bean Validation.
Separate business validation from request validation.
Use circuit breakers for unreliable services.
Handle partial failures in distributed workflows.
Maintain backward compatibility when changing APIs.
Design APIs that communicate failures clearly and consistently.
Every API receives input from external clients.
That input may be correct, incomplete, unexpected or deliberately manipulated.
Request validation checks whether incoming data satisfies the requirements of an API before the application processes it.
A. Why is request validation necessary?
A valid request might look like:
But what happens when a user submits:
Without validation, the application might attempt to store invalid information.
Checks whether required fields are present.
Example: A course must have a title.
Checks whether information follows the expected format.
Example: An email address must have a valid format.
Checks minimum and maximum field lengths.
Example: A course title cannot be longer than 150 characters.
Checks whether numerical values fall within acceptable boundaries.
Example: Course capacity cannot be negative.
Checks whether the supplied data has the expected type.
Example: availableSeats should be an integer, not an arbitrary text value.
Checks whether the request body contains the expected structure.
Convert incoming data into expected types
Check required fields, format and ranges
Validation should not be limited to the controller.
For example, a student submitting an enrolment request may provide a valid course ID, but that course may be full.
The request is structurally valid, but the operation is not valid according to the business rules.
You will learn why these different validation layers should work together.
Why this lesson matters: Request validation prevents invalid information from entering your application's business logic and database.
Validation and sanitization are related concepts, but they are not the same.
Validation determines whether an input is acceptable.
Sanitization transforms input into a safe or acceptable representation when transformation is appropriate.
Suppose an API accepts a student's email address.
You can validate the email format.
This does not satisfy the expected email format and should be rejected.
Sanitization is the controlled transformation of input.
For example, a platform that allows instructors to submit rich HTML course descriptions may need an HTML sanitizer to remove unsafe markup while retaining permitted formatting.
However, indiscriminately deleting special characters from every input is not a good security strategy.
It can corrupt legitimate information, such as names, languages, code examples or mathematical expressions.
Define exactly which input formats are permitted.
Example: A course status may only accept:
Limit strings, arrays, files and request sizes to reasonable values.
Encode output according to where it will be displayed, such as HTML, JavaScript, URLs or CSS.
This is an important defence against cross-site scripting (XSS).
Never construct SQL queries by directly concatenating untrusted input.
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'";
@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email") Optional<User> findByEmail( @Param("email") String email );
Actual file content and file signatures.
Do not rely only on the filename extension or the browser-provided MIME type.
Prevent unnecessarily large requests from consuming excessive memory or processing resources.
Suppose an application creates SQL using raw user input.
An attacker may submit malicious SQL fragments in an input field.
This can change the intended meaning of a database query.
Parameterized queries and ORM query binding help protect against this class of injection.
An attacker may attempt to submit malicious HTML or JavaScript that executes when another user opens a page.
For applications displaying user-generated content, you must understand HTML sanitization, contextual output encoding and Content Security Policy.
A course description may allow ordinary text and limited formatting but reject executable JavaScript.
Apply an appropriate HTML sanitization policy if rich HTML is supported.
Encode output correctly when displaying it.
Why this lesson matters: Good input handling protects databases, APIs and users without unnecessarily destroying legitimate application data.
In Spring Boot applications, Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) define the data accepted from clients and returned by APIs.
DTO validation allows you to define validation rules directly on request objects.
A DTO represents the information exchanged between application components or across an API boundary.
For example, a user registration request may need:
It should not expose internal database fields such as user ID, account creation timestamp or password hash for the client to control.
For a Maven-based Spring Boot application:
This provides Jakarta Bean Validation integration.
C. Creating a validated request DTO

import jakarta.validation.constraints.*; public record RegisterRequest( @NotBlank(message = "Name is required") @Size(max = 100, message = "Name is too long") String name, @NotBlank(message = "Email is required") @Email(message = "Invalid email format") String email, @NotBlank(message = "Password is required") @Size(min = 12, max = 128, message = "Password length must be between 12 and 128") String password ) {}
String cannot be null, empty or whitespace
String or collection cannot be empty
E. Applying validation in the controller

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/auth") public class RegistrationController { private final AuthService authService; public RegistrationController(AuthService authService) { this.authService = authService; } @PostMapping("/register") public ResponseEntity<?> register( @Valid @RequestBody RegisterRequest request) { authService.register(request); return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.CREATED) .body("Registration successful"); } }
The @Valid annotation triggers the validation rules.
If the request violates the constraints, Spring MVC raises a validation exception instead of allowing the controller operation to proceed normally.
Nested Validation: Validate objects inside other DTOs using @Valid.
Collection Validation: Validate lists of objects and their individual elements.
Custom Validation: Create custom annotations for application-specific rules.
Validation Groups: Apply different validation rules for create and update operations.
Cross-Field Validation: Validate relationships between multiple fields.
Example: An event's ending date must be later than its starting date.
You may implement this with a custom class-level constraint.
Why this lesson matters: DTO validation makes API contracts clearer, reduces repetitive validation code and produces consistent input requirements.
An API must handle errors gracefully.
Without centralized exception handling, different controllers may return different error formats for similar failures.
One controller returns a plain text error.
Another exposes a Java exception name.
Another accidentally returns an internal stack trace.
Exception handling is the mechanism through which an application detects and manages unexpected conditions during execution.
If the course does not exist, the backend should not return an uncontrolled exception.
It should return an appropriate HTTP response.
C. Local vs global exception handling
Local exception handling handles an error in a specific method using try-catch.
Global exception handling provides centralized handling for exceptions across controllers.
In Spring Boot, you commonly implement global handling using @RestControllerAdvice and @ExceptionHandler.
public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException { public ResourceNotFoundException(String message) { super(message); } }
Then define a global exception handler:

@RestControllerAdvice public class GlobalExceptionHandler { @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) public ResponseEntity<?> handleNotFound( ResourceNotFoundException ex) { return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) .body(Map.of( "error", "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND", "message", ex.getMessage() )); } @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) public ResponseEntity<?> handleUnexpected( Exception ex) { return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) .body(Map.of( "error", "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR", "message", "An unexpected error occurred" )); } }
This is a simplified starting point. A production implementation should also handle framework exceptions such as validation errors and ensure that sensitive exception details are not exposed.
Do not expose internal stack traces to clients.
Do not return database credentials or SQL details.
Log errors using an appropriate logging framework.
Include a trace or correlation ID for debugging.
Avoid catching every exception and pretending the operation succeeded.
Do not silently ignore important failures.
You will learn how exceptions travel through:
You will understand when an exception should be handled, when it should be translated into a domain-specific exception, and when it should propagate to a central handler.
Why this lesson matters: Global exception handling makes API failures consistent and prevents internal implementation details from leaking to users.
Lesson 5 — Designing Consistent API Error Responses
A professional API should communicate failures through a predictable response structure.
Frontend applications should not need to understand a different error format for every endpoint.
A. Why standard error responses matter
The frontend must implement different error-handling logic.
A standardized error format solves this problem.
B. Designing a common error structure
A useful error response might look like:

{ "type": "https://prepspaces.com/errors/validation", "title": "Validation Failed", "status": 400, "detail": "One or more fields contain invalid values", "instance": "/api/courses", "errorCode": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "traceId": "req-abc123", "fieldErrors": [ { "field": "title", "message": "Title is required" }, { "field": "availableSeats", "message": "Must be greater than zero" } ] }
Request path associated with the failure
Helps locate the error in application logs
D. RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs
You will study the standard Problem Details format defined by RFC 9457.
Spring Boot and Spring Framework support ProblemDetail, which can be used to build standardized error responses.

@ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleNotFound( ResourceNotFoundException ex) { ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail( HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage() ); problem.setTitle("Resource Not Found"); problem.setProperty( "errorCode", "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND" ); return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) .body(problem); }
Your API should return a clear list of validation failures.
You will learn to extract field errors from MethodArgumentNotValidException and include them in the standardized response.
F. Important API error design principles
Never expose internal exception messages indiscriminately.
Provide enough detail to help clients correct their requests.
Include a trace ID for support and debugging.
Keep error structures consistent across endpoints.
Avoid exposing sensitive data in error responses.
Why this lesson matters: Standardized errors make APIs easier to integrate, debug, test and maintain.
Request validation checks whether input is structurally correct.
Business logic validation checks whether an operation is allowed according to application rules.
This distinction is especially important in real-world backend systems.
The course ID is present and has the correct data type.
The student may already be enrolled.
The student may not have permission to enrol.
Student must not already be enrolled
Student must have access to the course
Enrolment must exist and be cancellable

@Service public class EnrollmentService { private final UserRepository userRepository; private final CourseRepository courseRepository; private final EnrollmentRepository enrollmentRepository; public EnrollmentService( UserRepository userRepository, CourseRepository courseRepository, EnrollmentRepository enrollmentRepository) { this.userRepository = userRepository; this.courseRepository = courseRepository; this.enrollmentRepository = enrollmentRepository; } @Transactional public Enrollment enroll(Long userId, Long courseId) { User user = userRepository.findById(userId) .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("User not found") ); Course course = courseRepository.findById(courseId) .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Course not found") ); if (course.getAvailableSeats() <= 0) { throw new BusinessException( "Course has no available seats" ); } if (enrollmentRepository .existsByUserIdAndCourseId(userId, courseId)) { throw new BusinessException( "Student is already enrolled" ); } // Persist enrollment and update seat count safely. return enrollmentRepository.save( new Enrollment(user, course) ); } }

This illustrates business validation. A real implementation must also address the concurrency problem between checking capacity, creating the enrolment and updating available seats. Module 04 introduced the database constraints and transaction techniques needed for that.
You will learn to create meaningful application exceptions such as:
These exceptions represent business failures rather than low-level technical problems.
E. Business validation vs database constraints
A business validation checks whether an operation is allowed.
A database constraint ensures that invalid data cannot be committed.
Service layer checks whether an email already exists.
Database unique constraint prevents duplicates even when concurrent requests bypass the initial check.
Why this lesson matters: Correct business validation prevents technically valid requests from performing operations that violate application rules.
Lesson 7 — Idempotency and Duplicate Request Prevention
This is one of the most important concepts in reliable API engineering.
Users may accidentally submit the same request multiple times. Networks may fail after the backend has already processed a request. Mobile applications may retry operations automatically.
Without duplicate-request protection, the same operation may execute multiple times.
An operation is idempotent if repeating the same operation produces the same intended result as performing it once.
For example, setting a user's course completion percentage to 50 is conceptually idempotent when repeated with the same value.
Creating a payment or submitting an enrolment may not be naturally idempotent.
The backend successfully creates the enrolment, but the response is lost because of a network interruption.
The frontend does not know whether the operation succeeded.
Without protection, the backend might process the same operation twice.
C. What is an idempotency key?
An idempotency key is a unique identifier supplied by the client to identify a logical operation.
The backend stores the key and the result of the operation.
When the same request arrives again with the same key, the backend can return the original result instead of executing the operation again.
Process the operation and save the result
The key should be unique within the appropriate scope, such as a user or client and endpoint.
Requests with the same key but different payloads.
Requests that fail halfway through processing.
Requests whose original outcome is unknown.
External payment or AI provider calls.
For simultaneous requests, an atomic database insert or unique constraint should determine which request owns the key.
If the same key is reused with a different request body, reject it rather than treating the second operation as an identical retry.
For long-running operations, you also need to manage an in-progress state and define what happens when a request becomes stuck.
HTTP method semantics are a useful starting point, but the actual behaviour depends on how the endpoint is implemented.
Why this lesson matters: Idempotency prevents duplicate payments, enrolments, orders and other operations when requests are retried.
A public API can receive requests from normal users, automated scripts, bots or malicious clients.
If a backend accepts unlimited requests, it may become overloaded.
Rate limiting controls how frequently clients can access an API.
Rate limiting restricts the number of requests allowed within a specific period.
Login API: 5 failed attempts per minute per account/IP policy Public course API: 100 requests per minute per client Expensive AI API: 10 requests per minute per user
These are illustrative policies. Actual limits should be designed according to application capacity and user experience.
B. Why is rate limiting necessary?
Login endpoints may be attacked using brute-force attempts.
Public APIs may receive excessive automated traffic.
AI endpoints may consume expensive provider resources.
Legitimate users may experience slow responses.
Counts requests within a fixed time window.
Its disadvantage is that users can send a burst near the boundary between two windows.
Records request timestamps and calculates usage over a moving time period.
It is more accurate but may require more storage.
Combines information from adjacent time windows to approximate a moving limit with less storage.
A bucket contains tokens. Requests consume tokens, and tokens are replenished at a defined rate.
It allows controlled bursts while maintaining an average request rate.
Requests enter a queue or bucket and are processed at a controlled rate.
Allow when a token is available
Tokens return at the configured rate
E. Rate limiting in distributed systems
If your application runs on multiple backend instances, storing counters only in local memory is insufficient.
Request 1 → Backend A Request 2 → Backend B Request 3 → Backend C
Each instance might maintain a separate counter and collectively exceed the intended limit.
You can use Redis for shared rate-limiting state.
When a client exceeds the limit:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: 30 Content-Type: application/json
{ "errorCode": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED", "message": "Too many requests. Please try again later." }
You will also learn about standard rate-limit response headers and how to communicate reset information.
Never blindly trust a client-supplied IP address or forwarding header. Configure trusted proxies so that rate limits cannot easily be bypassed by spoofing headers.
Why this lesson matters: Rate limiting protects backend resources, improves availability and helps prevent abusive API usage.
External services sometimes become slow or unavailable.
What happens if one of these services takes 60 seconds to respond?
Without timeouts and appropriate failure handling, backend resources can become occupied while waiting for a service that may never respond.
A timeout defines the maximum time an operation is allowed to wait.
Connection Timeout: Maximum time allowed to establish a connection.
Read Timeout: Maximum time allowed to wait for response data.
Write Timeout: Maximum time allowed to send data, where supported by the client.
Request Deadline: Total time allowed for the complete operation, including multiple downstream calls.
Suppose PrepSpaces requests an AI-generated interview evaluation.
The backend calls an external AI provider.
If the provider does not return within the configured time limit, the backend stops waiting and handles the failure according to its fallback policy.
The user should receive a meaningful response rather than waiting indefinitely.
Retry means attempting an operation again after a temporary failure.
Request 1 → Timeout Request 2 → Temporary connection failure Request 3 → Success
Retries can help when a service experiences temporary network issues.
However, retrying every failed request is dangerous.
This can be useful for very short, temporary conditions, but repeated immediate retries can overload the service.
Wait a predefined period before retrying.
Increase the waiting period after every failed attempt.
Add randomness to retry delays to avoid many clients retrying simultaneously.
This is especially important when a large number of clients experience the same service failure.
Operations where repeating the request could create another side effect.
For non-idempotent operations, use a reliable idempotency mechanism before retrying.
RetryConfig config = RetryConfig.custom() .maxAttempts(3) .waitDuration(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .retryExceptions(IOException.class) .build(); Retry retry = Retry.of("aiService", config);

This demonstrates the basic configuration. A production retry policy should distinguish retryable from non-retryable failures and account for deadlines, backoff, jitter and the downstream provider's rules.
Imagine ten backend instances simultaneously retry a failing service five times.
The failing service suddenly receives fifty additional requests.
This can make the outage worse.
Why this lesson matters: Timeouts prevent indefinite waiting, while carefully designed retries help recover from temporary failures without amplifying outages.
Retries are useful when a failure is temporary.
But what happens if an external service is completely unavailable?
Continuously retrying it can waste resources and make the situation worse.
A circuit breaker prevents repeated calls to a service that is consistently failing.
A. What is a circuit breaker?
A circuit breaker monitors calls to an external service.
When the failure rate exceeds a configured threshold, the circuit opens and temporarily prevents further calls.
This gives the failing service an opportunity to recover.
The circuit breaker blocks calls to the failing service.
Requests fail quickly or use an explicitly designed fallback.
After a configured waiting period, the circuit breaker allows a limited number of test requests.
If the service recovers, the circuit closes.
If the service continues failing, it opens again.
Fast failure instead of repeated downstream requests
Check whether the service has recovered
Imagine PrepSpaces uses an external AI provider to evaluate interview answers.
PrepSpaces Backend | v AI Provider | v Interview Evaluation
But the AI provider starts returning repeated errors.
The circuit breaker detects the failures and opens.
Instead of repeatedly calling the unavailable provider, the backend can:
Use a suitable alternative provider when one is configured.
Queue the work for later processing.
Offer a retry option to the user.
A fallback should never fabricate a successful evaluation.
E. Implementing circuit breakers with Resilience4j

CircuitBreakerConfig config = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom() .failureRateThreshold(50) .slidingWindowSize(10) .minimumNumberOfCalls(5) .waitDurationInOpenState( Duration.ofSeconds(30) ) .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(2) .build(); CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker = CircuitBreaker.of("aiProvider", config);
These are illustrative settings, not universal production defaults.
Usually works over a limited number of attempts
Tracks failure behaviour over a time window
You will also study how retries, circuit breakers and timeouts work together without creating conflicting behaviour.
Why this lesson matters: Circuit breakers help prevent one failing external dependency from continuously damaging the rest of your application.
Real backend systems frequently perform operations involving multiple services or databases.
Some operations may succeed while others fail.
This is known as a partial failure.
Imagine a student purchases a paid course.
In a monolithic application, multiple database operations may be coordinated using a single database transaction.
However, once an operation spans multiple independent services, a traditional database transaction cannot usually coordinate every operation.
Payment Service | v Enrollment Service | v Notification Service
Each service may maintain its own database and have independent availability.
A Saga is a pattern used to coordinate a multi-step business process across multiple services.
Instead of using one distributed database transaction, each step performs a local transaction.
If a later step fails, the system may execute compensating actions.
Compensation does not always mean perfectly reversing an operation. Some side effects, such as a delivered email, cannot be undone.
D. Understanding the Transactional Outbox Pattern
Suppose your application updates a database record and needs to publish an event.
Now the database has changed, but downstream services were never notified.
The Transactional Outbox Pattern addresses this.
An event record in an outbox table.
Both writes occur in one database transaction.
A separate publisher reads the outbox and delivers the events.
Reads pending events and publishes them
Message delivery may happen more than once, so event consumers should be idempotent.
Compensating Transactions: Reverse or offset a previously completed business operation.
Eventual Consistency: Allow different services to become consistent over time rather than requiring every service to update simultaneously.
Dead-Letter Queues: Store messages that repeatedly fail processing for investigation or later recovery.
Idempotent Consumers: Ensure that consuming the same event more than once does not duplicate its business effect.
Graceful Degradation: Keep essential features operational when optional dependencies fail.
Queue-Based Processing: Move long-running or unreliable work into asynchronous jobs.
Why this lesson matters: Distributed systems cannot assume that every operation will succeed simultaneously. Reliable applications need recovery mechanisms for incomplete workflows.
You may add new fields, change data structures, introduce new features or remove old functionality.
But changing an API can break applications that depend on its previous behaviour.
Imagine PrepSpaces has a frontend deployed on multiple devices and older browser sessions are still active.
The old frontend expects id and title.
This is an API compatibility problem.
Backward compatibility means newer versions of an API continue supporting existing clients and integrations to the extent promised by the API contract.
Even seemingly harmless changes can be breaking if clients depend on the previous behaviour.
One common method is URL-based versioning.
Version 1 remains available while clients gradually migrate to version 2.
Other approaches include versioning through media types or headers.
You will compare the trade-offs of different approaches.
You will learn how this helps communicate release changes.
Deprecation means an API feature is still supported but is scheduled for removal or replacement.
Remove the old endpoint after the transition.
You will study HTTP deprecation and sunset signalling, including the relevant Deprecation and Sunset response headers.
Contract testing checks whether API providers and consumers agree on the structure and behaviour of an API.
Why this lesson matters: API compatibility allows backend teams to improve their systems without unexpectedly breaking existing users and integrations.
4. Practical Lab — Make an Existing API Reliable
In this lab, you will take an existing Spring Boot REST API and improve its validation, error handling, idempotency, traffic control and failure recovery.
You should use the course-enrolment API developed in earlier modules as your starting application.
The initial API contains several deliberately introduced reliability problems.
Invalid request data can reach service methods.
Different endpoints return different error formats.
Duplicate enrolment requests create duplicate operations.
External service calls can wait indefinitely.
Partial operations are not handled correctly.
API changes are not documented or versioned.
Your task is to fix these problems.
Shared rate-limit and idempotency state, where appropriate
Create DTOs for course and enrolment requests.

public record EnrollmentRequest( @NotNull(message = "User ID is required") @Positive(message = "User ID must be positive") Long userId, @NotNull(message = "Course ID is required") @Positive(message = "Course ID must be positive") Long courseId ) {}
D. Step 2 — Add Global Exception Handling
Include field-specific validation errors when applicable.
A student cannot enrol twice in the same course.
A full course cannot accept another enrolment.
A cancelled enrolment cannot be completed.
Only authorised users can perform restricted operations.
Use service-level validation and database constraints together.
Modify the enrolment endpoint to support:
Generate or receive a unique idempotency key.
Store the key and request fingerprint.
Return the original result for valid retries.
Reject key reuse with different request data.
Ensure database writes are transactionally consistent.
Test the endpoint by submitting the same request multiple times.
G. Step 5 — Add API Rate Limiting
5 failed attempts per minute under an account/IP policy
These are sample policies for the exercise.
Use Redis or a suitable shared rate-limiting service so that the limits work across multiple application instances.
Return 429 Too Many Requests with useful retry information.
H. Step 6 — Add Timeouts and Retries
Assume your application calls an external service.
Test both temporary failures and permanent failures.
Do not automatically retry a non-idempotent operation.
I. Step 7 — Implement a Circuit Breaker
Use Resilience4j to protect calls to an unreliable external service.
Test the behaviour by deliberately simulating service failures.
Add a scenario where enrolment creation triggers a notification event.
Save a notification event in the outbox.
Prevent consumers from processing the same event twice.
Demonstrate that enrolment data remains consistent even when notification delivery fails.
K. Step 9 — API Documentation and Compatibility
Then make a compatible improvement or introduce a new version without unexpectedly breaking existing clients.
5. Assignment — Make a Deliberately Unreliable API Predictable
You have been provided with a fictional backend API that works under normal conditions but frequently fails under unexpected conditions.
The API suffers from invalid requests, duplicate operations, inconsistent errors, uncontrolled traffic, timeouts and partial failures.
Your task is to transform this unreliable API into a predictable, fault-tolerant backend.
Inspect the application and identify at least these problems:
Document how each issue affects users and application reliability.
Part B — Validation and Error Handling
Part C — Idempotency and Rate Limiting
Design a workflow involving at least two services.
A failure in a later operation.
Transactional outbox or another reliable event-delivery mechanism.
Create two versions of an API.
Write automated tests for normal and failure conditions.
After completing the lab and assignment, you should be able to reason about these situations.
A student clicks Enrol twice, but the first response is delayed. How will your API ensure that the student is enrolled only once?
Your application creates a record, but the next database operation fails. How will you prevent inconsistent data?
An external AI provider begins returning errors for every request. How will timeouts, retries and circuit breakers prevent your backend from becoming overloaded?
A bot sends thousands of requests to your public course endpoint. How will you protect backend resources without blocking legitimate students?
A payment provider confirms a payment, but your enrolment service is temporarily unavailable. How will you recover without charging the student again?
Your message broker delivers the same enrolment event three times. How will your notification service prevent duplicate emails or repeated business operations?
Challenge 7 — API update breaks the frontend
You rename an existing response field, and an older frontend version stops working. How will you introduce the change without disrupting existing clients?
Your backend has ten application instances, and every instance retries a failing external API. How will you prevent retries from making the outage worse?
These challenges test whether you understand reliability as a system-design responsibility rather than just writing try-catch blocks.
Throughout this module, follow these principles:
Validate incoming data before processing it.
Do not confuse input validation with business validation.
Never rely on sanitization as a universal replacement for validation and output encoding.
Keep error responses consistent across the application.
Never expose internal stack traces or sensitive implementation details.
Use database constraints to enforce critical data rules.
Apply rate limits according to the cost and risk of each endpoint.
Use circuit breakers to protect against sustained downstream failures.
Design recovery strategies for partial failures.
Test the failure paths, not just successful requests.
For deeper study, explore these official resources:
[Resilience4j Documentation](https://resilience4j.readme.io/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — retry, circuit breaker and bulkhead patterns.
By the end of Module 06, you should understand that building a successful API is not simply about returning 200 OK when everything works.

You will know how to handle invalid input, communicate failures, prevent duplicate operations, control excessive traffic, recover from temporary service interruptions, protect against cascading failures and evolve APIs without unexpectedly breaking their consumers.
You will also understand how reliability techniques work together:
Circuit breakers protect against unavailable services.
Your final objective: Be able to transform a basic REST API into a predictable, maintainable and resilient backend service that handles both normal operations and unexpected failures reliably.
